style_prompt:
Style: Warm, grounded Alaska public radio. Curious rather than alarmed, because nothing has been decided yet and this is an investigation, not a verdict. Plain spoken, a dry half smile on the opening lines, real respect on every person and institution quoted, someone working out a bill at a kitchen table through the middle, and genuine hope on the final sentence. Never sour, never a sales pitch, and never sardonic about anyone.
Pace: MEASURED and unhurried. THIS IS A TWO MINUTE PIECE, about one hundred and twenty seconds, and the read must FILL it, so give every sentence room to land and take a real breath at every period. Do not rush the numbers. Vary the tone line to line so no two sentences sound the same.
Emphasis: Lean on the one key word in each line and let the numbers land. The question near the top is a real question a person is asking, not a setup. The line about Fairbanks asking for a pause is a plain civic note, the driest line in that stretch. The line about a partnership supporting Airmen and Guardians is the other side's honest case and is read straight, with respect and no irony at all. The two sentences about the land and the power are the quietest in the piece, with a real beat between them. The fighter wing line and the data center line are two separate thoughts, not one breath. The last sentence is hopeful, an opening and not a defeat.
Pronunciation: A I is the two letters, ay-eye. Eielson is EEL-son. Salcha is SAL-chuh. Murkowski is mer-KOW-skee. Grier is GREER. F thirty fives is eff thirty fives.

lines.text: The Air Force is offering about four thousand seven hundred acres of Alaska for A I data centers.
lines.pace: baseline, a small settle on the number
lines.why: The number is enormous and the read does not sell it. Flat and factual with a half smile is what makes it land, and it leaves the ladder room to move both ways from here.

lines.text: Some sits at Eielson Air Force Base, outside Fairbanks, where bills are among the nation's highest.
lines.pace: baseline, slight weight on the last clause
lines.why: Drop under line zero so the lift into the question has somewhere to come from. The stake for a Fairbanks household arrives quietly, which is how a stake earns belief.

lines.text: Does that shrink a Fairbanks bill or grow it? One number decides. The offering doesn't say.
lines.pace: forward and genuinely asking, then a full stop and a hard, level landing on the last sentence
lines.why: This is the film's one question and it has to sound genuinely asked, so the lift is real. The cold drop on the offering doesn't say is directed in the notes rather than tagged, because the period plus a level landing does the job and costs no runtime.

lines.text: Nothing's awarded. [wry] Alaskans took positions anyway.
lines.why: The half smile is earned here and nowhere else in the open. Dropping off the hook's four keeps the contrast and hands the testimony block a clean floor to start from. The tag is mid-line after a period, never line-initial.

lines.text: Salcha resident Sarah Hollister told reporters the jets always meant sacrifice.
lines.why: A quoted Alaskan gets respect, not a jeer. Sitting low here makes the next line's rise read as her feeling rather than as the narrator's opinion.

lines.text: Swap that for a data center's hum, she said, and we've lost our way.
lines.pace: a touch slower on the last clause, weight not volume
lines.why: The emotional peak of the first half. Weight rather than heat, because the film is carrying her conviction, not endorsing or mocking it.

lines.text: Fairbanks asked for a pause, on both its state and federal lists.
lines.pace: plain, dry, matter of fact, no colour at all
lines.why: The third testimony voice is an institution filing paperwork, and the flatness is the point: a town's formal ask sounds nothing like a neighbour on a trail, and the contrast right after the emotional peak is what makes both read as true.

lines.text: Senator Lisa Murkowski says Alaska can't support them on an insecure energy base.
lines.pace: even, let the full name land clean
lines.why: Level and reportorial, lifting just off the civic note. Insecure is the load-bearing word because it names the input, which is exactly what the hinge is about to point at.

lines.text: She didn't say the land. [short pause] She said the power.
lines.pace: slow, deliberate, the quietest line in the film
lines.why: The hinge of the whole piece. Dropping from three to one is the biggest move on the ladder, and a real beat between the two sentences is what turns a sentence into a realisation. This is one of only two pause tags in the film, because this is where a beat is worth its seconds.

lines.text: The Air Force calls it a partnership supporting its Airmen and Guardians.
lines.pace: straight, even, generous, absolutely no lift of the eyebrow
lines.why: This is the other side's honest case and the film means it. Read with irony it makes the whole piece a hit and the thesis dies, so the delivery here is the plainest kind of respect: state it as the institution states it, and let the audience weigh it.

lines.text: Your bill is wires and fuel. The wires split across everyone, so that half is tall.
lines.pace: conversational and close, a person explaining at a kitchen table
lines.why: Coming down and in changes the room from testimony to arithmetic. Tall is the picture the viewer is watching get drawn, so the voice hands it over rather than announcing it.

lines.text: A giant customer helps pay for them either way. That half thins.
lines.pace: lift on either way, then settle onto thins
lines.why: Either way carries the entire logical load of the film, because it is the one thing in the bill that does not depend on the missing number. The jump from two to four is what marks it without a tag.

lines.text: The fuel bites. A big load either brings its own power, or competes for what's here.
lines.pace: even, hold the fork level in the second sentence, do not favour either branch
lines.why: Bites is the turn from settled to unsettled. Dropping back off four keeps the fork neutral, which the angle requires: the film never narrates which branch is likelier.

lines.text: So it turns on how big. And how big is what nobody has published.
lines.pace: noticeably slower through the second sentence, quiet rather than loud
lines.why: The reveal the whole diagram was built for. It is slowed by direction rather than by a tag this time, to keep the runtime off the ceiling, and quiet beats loud here anyway because the subject of the sentence is an absence.

lines.text: Mayor Grier Hopkins says defense spending buoyed Fairbanks when the F thirty fives came.
lines.pace: warmer and more open than anything before it
lines.why: The warmest moment in the film and genuine credit to a town that made a good bet once. The lift from two is what tells the audience this is not the setup for a dunk.

lines.text: But a fighter wing comes with a budget. [short pause] A data center comes with an appetite.
lines.pace: slow and separated, two thoughts and not one breath
lines.why: The best line in the script, and it only works if the halves are not rushed together. Settling under the warmth of fourteen lets the last word do the work. The second and last pause tag in the film.

lines.text: So the ask isn't megawatts. Nobody can publish those yet.
lines.why: This is the concession the angle insists on, so it has to sound like the film conceding rather than the film scolding. Low and generous, which also clears the runway for the ask.

lines.text: Ask for the date. Does that number go public before the land is leased?
lines.pace: direct and level, the plainest delivery in the piece, a real question mark at the end without singsong
lines.why: The film's actual instruction. Level and direct to camera, because an instruction that sounds performed sounds optional.

lines.text: The terms aren't written. That's the opening.
lines.pace: settle, warm lift on the final word
lines.why: The whole film turns on that last word sounding hopeful rather than grim. Unwritten terms are the good news, so the tone rises into opening instead of falling off it.
